newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada T-bills open stronger, rate hike fears wane.
newsitem.headline: Canada T-bills open stronger, rate hike fears wane.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened stronger on Wednesday, boosted by some overseas buying, as a strengthening dollar reduced speculation that the central bank would soon hike rates, dealers said.

"It (the dollar strength) is definitely benefiting. That's really what the market seems to be focused on right now. The reason that the market had backed up to the extent that it has is paranoia regarding the bank tightening," said one dealer with a bank-owned brokerage.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.35 percent from 3.36 percent at Tuesday's close.
Canadian T-bills had softened over the past week as weakness in the Canadian dollar increased speculation the Bank of Canada would hike rates for a second time this year.
However, Canada's dollar opened firmer on Wednesday at C$1.3835 (US$0.7228) lifted by interest to buy on the back of Australia's fifth rate cut in a year.
Dealers said today's strength is also partly the continuation of gains the money market began making yesterday afternoon after the weekly T-bill tender saw good buying interest.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.73 percent from 3.74 percent on Tuesday. The one-year when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 4.21 percent from 4.24 percent.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.30 percent, near the middle of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range.
